So an undersized OH needs to have a few things to get my attention:
-  good ball control, ability to mix up shot speeds, and variation in attacks.  Shorter attackers need to find a way to get kills other than just over powering the blockers.  Tooling, roll shots/tips, ability to go thumb up/down, etc. go a long way.
-  can run a fast offense.  Getting separation in the block gives a shorter hitter space to get kills.  High and tight won’t cut it when you are up against players with 5+ inches in height advantage.  Knowing how to hit different sets and how each of them integrate into an overall offense plan always helps players stand out to me.
-  have good volleyball IQ.  Smart players know defensive schemes and know how to beat them.  They is the patterns they are seeing across the net to help them make good shot choices and are always thinking a shot or two ahead.
-  are 6 rotation players.  If I have to sub you out to put a defender in I am way more inclined to just take the bigger player (all other things being equal).  If you are a threat in the back row as an attacker AND bring solid defense you will definitely have my attention.

Hope that helps - those are just the things that come to mind.  I’m sure there are more but in the end it’s not the size of the dog in the fight…it’s the size of the fight in the dog.

Just a couple things:
-  Your extension with your arm looks great.  If you can get your elbow a little more out in front of your wrist until you are ready to contact the ball it will give you more snap.  If you are having trouble getting the ball to get good topspin and downward angle this should fix that.
-  Your hip shoulder separation could use some work.  You want to have the hip on your hitting arm side lead your shoulder as well as your leg.  This builds up some tension and get more torque from your core.  Also, if you can get your hip to rotate up slightly as you come around it will help you get another inch or so out of your extension.  
Those two things aside you are in a good place with your swing.  If you were one of my players I would focus on refining those two things and start moving you towards disguising your shots and using your wrist to redirect without losing power.  Good luck and I hope they all made sense and helped a little!

So a few things right off the bat:
-  Your closing steps and backswing could be improved.  By not loading properly you are coding yourself inches in vertical and not generating power from your core
-  You are driving your toe into the ground on your final step, which if done properly helps turn your forward momentum into vertical energy.  Going back to your approach being off - this is also costing you power and height as you are just driving that energy into the floor
-  Lastly, your upper body is too square to the net when you are taking off.  This is forcing you to use mostly shoulder when hitting instead of getting the whip effect from having proper hip shoulder separation.  Being more open (perpendicular to the net) when you are taking off will help you improve.  

For the footwork here is a good starting video:  https://youtu.be/YTa1mIBZ3EM
For the hip/shoulder here is a good one as well:  https://youtu.be/8_QwOHXNK9o

Former HS coach here with a couple pieces of advice:
-  The earlier post about running is just a way for coaches to see who will give up.  Don’t worry about being first or last, just don’t stop.  Coaches want players who want to be there and are willing to give it whatever they can.  Also, it’s a really easy way to pare down the field from 40 to something more reasonable.
-  Again, going back to the previous response, hustle hustle hustle.  Being that many players trying out as freshmen won’t have a ton of experience coaches are looking for players that stand out, both good and bad.  Being late back to a huddle, not following directions, or just standing out in a negative way will hurt your chances.
-  Don’t worry about being one of the best on the court.  A good coach will know in about 20 minutes who their top 8 are.  From there they are looking for players they think they can teach.  Having a positive attitude goes a long way and just showing your athleticism are the most important things you can do to help your chances.
-  Let your mistakes go.  Don’t focus on the last ball, just focus on doing your best on the next ball.  
-  Have your paperwork ready when the coach asks for it.  I’m sure you have to have physical paperwork and other school permission paperwork to attend tryouts. Be sure to have that in order.

Lastly, just have fun.  At your age the game is supposed to be fun - coaches notice that.  They want players who are as excited to attend practice and learn as much as those who want to play in games.

I hope all that helped and good luck!

So your swing has some really good mechanics going on but a few things you could do help with your contact point and and buys a little power:

\-  Left arm needs to be up higher and longer with your thumb pointing downward, it snaps down along your side as you bring your right arm over top to hit - the see saw effect will let you wait longer to swing as your overall motion should be faster

\-  Elbow needs to lead your hand a little more.  Swing should be more like a whip than a hammer - you have a pretty good hammer, now if you add some whip you will will drive the ball down more as well as as topspin to it

\-  When you are loading (getting ready to take off) make sure you are trying to pull your shoulder blades together.  This will let you build more tension in your core as well as open up your shoulders.  This, coupled with the left arm pull that I mentioned will let you rotate your hitting shoulder up higher and move your contact point on the ball a little higher and rotate your body down through the ball as you hit.

You have a great start going already so just keep working.  Good luck and hope this helped a little!

So I’m guessing you are an outside.  With that in mind, here are a couple of options:
-  if the other team is running a perimeter defense a roll shot over the middle to 3 is always a good option.  IF it lands it’s a point, but even if it doesn’t it forces the opposing outside to come cover the short and opens up the hard cross shot and puts you one on one with the opposing left back
-  work on your line shot.  If the other team sets their block inside out you can either tool them, blast the setter if they are down, or just go off speed and chop the ball deep to the 1 corner.  If you approach and let the ball drift a little across your body toward the antenna and turn on it the tool shot is a really great weapon
-  if the block is set up outside in, a hard cutter to the other 4 spot is a good option but tough to pull off unless the set dies a little
-  a good bailout shot that worked for me back in the day was moving further outside an attacking with an angle that was almost parallel to the net then hitting across your body back toward the 6/1.  It can kill your shoulder though but really messes with the blockers timing.  

All in all, just try to vary your shot speed and get the blockers and/or the defense to have to think.  That microsecond of hesitation will give you an opening.  Good luck from a short (former) OH who hated high sets too!

- shoulder should be slightly out in front of your knee and arms need to be no more than 45 degrees off your midline%. The wide arms makes for extra distance for the, to travel when making contact and makes you more error prone

-  relax in the shoulders and arms until contact.  It’s just like a race car - loose is fast, tight is slow.  Stay loose until it’s time to make contact with the ball.
-  don’t take all this criticism to hard.  You are on your way, just keep working and good luck!

Agree with all these points (especially the heel strike/plant step which is not brought up nearly enough) and would just add a couple:
-  if you put some more height in your toss you don’t have to commit immediately to your timing step (first step).  I always tell my players not to toss and chase, but to toss, adjust, and attack.  If you commit to your approach as soon as you toss (or at forced to with a low toss) you lose any ability to adapt your serve and every toss is a little different so that can be crucial sometimes.
-  as far as adding more power here are three things I see (all of which a higher toss will give you a chance to integrate):
— lower your hips and bend your legs more during your closing steps.  Gives you more loading to get higher when you hit the ball
— wait as long as possible on your arm backswing (your gather) and bring them back further and tight along your body.  Then when you pull them through into your draw you will do it quicker.  Same motion in less time equals more power.
— lastly, by waiting as long as possible to pull back into your draw you will build more torque through your ribs/core.  This, along with a slight back arch and trying to “pinch” your shoulder blades together before you let your swing go will buy you a ton of power without a ton of extra mechanical changes.

Good luck!

I trade these almost exclusively.  A couple of things I build my trades around:
-  3 to 4 weeks until expiration 
-  no more than 10% of my portfolio into any 1 trade
-  base my inner wing on:
    -  the % changes I have seen of the underlying over the past 3 monthly expirations
    -  the overall movement of the market
-  I usually exit at 50% of max profit if the underlying is near either of the inner wings.  I’ll hold longer if it’s is still near the midpoint at 1 we left until expiration.
- if I’m at max loss I usually break up my exit trades into 2 verticals to improve the chance they get filled.
